 Here's When Election Results Will Be Finalized Across the Country 
 Races may be called on November 3, but results won’t be official in some states until December.
 Oct. 29, 2026 •  
 Carl Smith 
 Facebook 
 LinkedIn 
 Twitter 
 Email 
 Print 
 Early voting at Bladensburg Elementary School in Prince George's County, Maryland. (Mennatalla Ibrahim/TNS) 
 It's a turbulent midterm year when three or four races could shift the balance of power in each house of Congress. Mail voting has come under fire as the president has tried to institute sweeping changes to the practice via executive order. His attempts have been stymied in the courts, but may have created some measure of confusion among voters about exactly when their mail ballots must arrive to their destination.
Twelve states will count mail in ballots received after Nov. 3, as long as they are postmarked by Election Day (see map). Washington has the most generous grace period, accepting mail ballots until Nov. 23. As postal service cuts have created uncertainty about timely service, especially in rural areas , it's important for voters to know their state's policies.
The long counting period in Washington could open the door to challenges in a fraught year when the Trump administration has already begun laying the groundwork for casting doubt on unfavorable results ; the House race in the Washington’s third Congressional District is among those being watched closely. It’s a competitive race where Democrats are counting on the incumbent, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, to hold her seat.
States also certify results at different times. The certification deadline in Oklahoma, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming is Nov. 10 (the races in these states aren't set to potentially shift the balance of power in Washington). But Senate contests in Iowa, Nebraska and Texas combine “must-win” status and longer than average certification deadlines — Dec. 7 for Texas and Nov. 30 for the other states.
It’s hard to know in advance where and how results might be challenged along the way to certification. “The Department of Justice has filed a preemptive challenge of Alaska’s Senate election, arguing that if the Democratic candidate wins it could be because voters confused the Republican incumbent with another candidate who has an almost identical name.
There’s more time for this in Alaska than in some other states; the state certifies results on Nov. 25.
Attorney General Todd Blanche caught the attention election officials this week when he was asked at a press conference whether the Department of Justice might attempt to prevent certification of results in state elections.
“It is not DOJ’s intention — and it’s never our intention — to improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process,” he said , “but to say that there’s no circumstances that we would ever do that — of course I’m not going to say that.”
